\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Main Comparison}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity across methods and seeds.
Adaptive reweighting achieves mean PPL 17.651, matching grid-best ($b{=}0.5$, mean 17.646) within seed-to-seed variance: the per-seed gap never exceeds 0.007, less than half the cross-seed range of the uniform baseline (17.686--17.702).
This parity comes at zero validation cost---grid search requires $|\mathcal{B}|$ complete training runs (six in our sweep), whereas adaptive requires one.

The grid-$b$ sweep reveals monotonically increasing PPL from $b{=}0.5$ to $b{=}5.0$ (17.651 to 17.818 on seed 42; full sweep in Appendix~\ref{app:grid}), confirming that exponent selection is consequential.
The optimal $b{=}0.5$ differs from the $b{=}10$ reported by \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} at comparable model scale, underscoring the model-dependence of fixed-exponent selection.

ESS-only (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.723 across three seeds, \emph{worse} than uniform (17.694) by 0.029.
Removing $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and maximizing $b$ subject only to $\mathrm{ESS} \geq n_{\min}$ leads to over-downweighting that degrades training, providing direct evidence for the minimum-intervention principle.

The Golden Ratio oracle~\citep{he_2025_golden_ratio} achieves PPL 17.654 on seed 42 using known provenance labels.
Adaptive reaches within 0.001 of this upper bound without provenance access, suggesting the dual constraint recovers near-optimal weights from noisy detector scores alone.

The adaptive $b^*$ distribution (median 0.87, IQR $[0.54, 1.51]$, mean 1.40) confirms that most batches need only moderate intervention.
The constraint regime breakdown in \S\ref{sec:algorithm} shows that $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ prevents over-intervention in the 40\% of reweighted batches where moderate $b$ already meets the quality target.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Seed 42} & \textbf{Seed 123} & \textbf{Seed 456} & \textbf{Mean} \\
\midrule
Uniform               & 17.694 & 17.686 & 17.702 & 17.694 \\
Grid-best ($b{=}0.5$) & \textbf{17.651} & \textbf{17.638} & \textbf{17.650} & \textbf{17.646} \\
ESS-only               & 17.730 & 17.720 & 17.719 & 17.723 \\
Golden Ratio$^\dagger$ & 17.654 & --     & --     & --     \\
\midrule
Adaptive (ours)        & 17.653 & 17.643 & 17.657 & 17.651 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Held-out perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$).
Grid-best selects the optimal fixed $b$ post-hoc from six candidates.
$^\dagger$Evaluated on seed 42 only.
Best per column in \textbf{bold}.}
\label{tab:main}
\end{table}

\subsection{Sensitivity Analysis}

file.content:
\paragraph{Training Data.}
We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo2024fineweb} as the real-data source.
To simulate web-scale synthetic contamination, we generate continuations with Qwen3-0.6B~\citep{yang2025qwen3}---the same model we continue pretraining---and inject them at ratio $\rho = 0.4$ via uniform random mixing.
This self-contamination design---where the model's own outputs are mixed back into its training data---creates a particularly challenging detection scenario, as generator and trainee share identical pretrained weights.

\paragraph{Detector.}
We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split, achieving AUC\,=\,0.939 with calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048 after temperature scaling ($T = 0.204$).
The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson2025detection}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} may matter as much as raw discrimination for reweighting.

\paragraph{Training.}
We continue pretraining Qwen3-0.6B for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, cosine schedule (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision.
The pretrained checkpoint starts at PPL\,=\,22.97 on our held-out set; after continued pretraining, the best method (adaptive $\bstar$) reaches $17.651 {\pm} 0.007$ across three seeds ($\Delta$PPL\,=\,$-5.319$, $-23.2\%$).
All main comparisons use three random seeds (42, 123, 456).
We note that method-level differences (${\sim}0.04$ PPL between adaptive and uniform) are small in absolute terms but arise in a regime where the model is already well-optimized; the $5{+}$ PPL drop from pretraining absorbs the easy gains, making further improvement from data curation increasingly difficult.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity (PPL) on a balanced real/synthetic test set via sliding-window evaluation (stride 1024, 4.08M tokens).
All evaluations are post-hoc with a unified pipeline; training involves no inline evaluation.

\paragraph{Methods.}
We compare five approaches:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Uniform}: $w_j = 1$ for all $j$ (no contamination handling).
  \item \textbf{Grid-$b$}: fixed $b \in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0\}$, best selected post-hoc by held-out PPL.
        Represents validation-based selection~\citep{drayson2025detection}.
  \item \textbf{ESS-only}: $b^* = \max\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$, the maximum-intervention variant retaining only the stability constraint, ablating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  \item \textbf{Golden Ratio}: $w = 1/\varphi \approx 0.618$ for synthetic ($q_j > 0.5$), $w = 1$ otherwise~\citep{he2025golden}.
        Requires known provenance labels (oracle).
  \item \textbf{Adaptive} (ours): per-batch $b^*$ from the dual-constraint formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}), with $\tau = 0.8$ and $n_{\min} = 2$ (half the micro-batch size).
\end{itemize}
